source.title: Do We Really Need a New Theory to Understand the Double-Descent?
source.authors: L. Oneto; S. Ridella; D. Anguita

record.tranche_reason: Reports empirical training-error results as model size varies, testing the general interpolation behavior with a different model family, training method, and data setting than the listed versions specify.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results for a toy polynomial regression problem and a shallow MNIST classifier. It does not test the listed CIFAR convolutional-network, teacher-student, depth, initialization, learning-rate, or batch-normalization conditions. Earlier cited results are not extracted as this paper’s results.
record.test_reason: The study measures interpolation and double descent in polynomial regression and a shallow random-feature MNIST classifier fitted by regularized least squares. Neither experiment tests gradient optimization in the systems specified by V1–V6. Algorithmic stability here measures sensitivity to replacing training samples, not the learning-rate stability in V5.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors argue that existing algorithmic stability theory helps explain double descent, support this with two empirical examples, and call for further theoretical analysis and empirical evidence.
record.recipe_differences: Uses regularized least squares with polynomial regression and a shallow ReLU MNIST classifier; it does not report the initialization or gradient-training recipes named in the versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Model size is varied; the first example uses a single round, with the authors saying results are consistent over repetitions and parameter changes.

fits_no_version.finding: Polynomial regression training error decreases to zero by the interpolation threshold as model size increases.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Increasing polynomial model size can permit interpolation in the reported regularized least-squares regression setup.

fits_no_version.finding: The authors describe the shallow random-feature MNIST experiment as confirming the preceding interpolation and double-descent results; exact training classification errors are not stated in prose.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A shallow random-feature classifier fitted by regularized least squares can exhibit interpolation and double descent as feature count increases.

record.peer_reviewed: The European Symposium on Artificial Neural Networks, Computational Intelligence and Machine Learning (ESANN 2022 proceedings)
record.problems: The empirical evidence is limited to two examples; the toy regression results are from a single round, and the MNIST training-error curve is described only as confirming the preceding results, without numerical values in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No additional qualifying results identified. Cited findings from other work and complexity/stability quantities are not results measuring training classification error for the versions listed.

untested.parts: Gradient-trained convolutional networks on CIFAR-10/100, including random or corrupted labels and the specified capacity, stopping, and regularization conditions.
ReLU teacher-student optimization, spurious local minima, and the effect of extra student neurons.
Training degradation with depth and comparisons involving identity shortcuts, special initialization, or normalization.
Initialization effects on gradient propagation, training speed, and trainable depth.
Learning-rate stability thresholds, curvature dynamics, recovery, edge-of-stability training, and divergence.
Batch normalization effects on training speed and learning-rate tolerance, including Fixup comparisons.

record.verdict_notes: The experiments are the study's own results, but their interpolation behavior does not test any listed claim version. The cannot_determine states concern those versions, not a denial of the reported polynomial interpolation result.

versions.untested_parts: CIFAR-10/100, convolutional networks, SGD or Adam, random initialization, corrupted or random labels, and the stated smaller-model, early-stopping, and regularization conditions.
Two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems, spurious minima, and student width relative to teacher width.
Depth, plain versus residual networks, shortcuts, normalization, and the stated ImageNet/CIFAR-10 settings.
Activation-matched and orthogonal initializations, signal/gradient propagation, and very deep tanh or convolutional networks.
Learning rates above stability limits, loss and curvature dynamics, sharpness, and divergence.
Batch normalization comparisons, training speed, learning-rate tolerance, and Fixup.

rows.value: decreases to zero until the interpolation threshold
rows.uncertainty: Results reported for a single round; text says results are quite consistent over repetitions and parameter changes.
rows.note: The paper reports the curve qualitatively in prose and says Figure 2 shows training error decreasing to zero until interpolation; it does not give a numerical value for each model size.
rows.check: The reported decrease to zero concerns polynomial regression error, not convolutional-network training classification error under SGD or Adam. The subject is a polynomial model, not a neural network. Distinguish the eight sampled observations from the varied polynomial degree/model size.

rows.operation_detail: Varied the number of ReLU units in regularized least squares and measured training classification error.

multiclass mapped into one-versus-all binary classification problems

rows.value: Figure 3 confirms the results and comments reported for Figure 2; no numerical values stated in text
rows.note: The text says Figure 3 confirms the Figure 2 results but does not state the MNIST training-error values or explicitly describe them reaching zero.
rows.check: This is a random-feature ReLU classifier with fixed sampled feature vectors and coefficients fitted by regularized least squares, not the gradient-trained convolutional networks in V1. MNIST inputs are in R^(28²), not R^28. The qualitative confirmation of Figure 2 does not establish a partial effect for any listed version; exact training-error values cannot be recovered reliably from the supplied figure text.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
